The last two questions (#22 – Why do you hate fat people? And #23 – What are your hobbies/interests (besides hating fat people)?) will still require some further work.

You could create separate categories (create a coding system) to put reoccurring themes in, and quantify your results that way. Ideally your themes/categories would be based on preexisting research to justify them but for a non-academic online thing you could just make categories up on your own. Another thing you can do is just write a summary of the most frequent reasons people bring up for why they hate fat people. There's an endless amount of ways to dissect open ended questions...so good luck with that ;)
Yeah, but it still needs to be done by hand. Cleaning data isn't hard, it's just time consuming. That's why we have interns and undergrads do it.

I think then writing a summary of the open ended questions is probably the best. Maybe use a couple examples to highlight interesting responses or unusual responses, as well as some examples/quotes that best represent the majority opinions from the open-ended.

There's a lot of ways to interpret the open-ended question even then...like, I'm sure a vast majority of responses can be separated into "attitudes" (e.g. fat people are disgusting, anger-inducing) vs more "factual" responses (fat people are unhealthy, cost taxpayer dollars, etc) vs whatever else is in there.

But it's not just what they think, it's what part of respondents agree with them. You could have an algorithm search for keyword pairs and triples, and look at their frquency and proximity to other kewords, among other factors, to categorize responses like a spam filter does email, but you still need a lot of data to train the algorithm, which still means going through the data by hand and categorizing the training data. The good thing is that next time around there will be known categories to work with, and whoever runs the survey can do a more straightforward analysis.
